title: Anyone use Claude-Code-Game-Studios suite?
author: FondantIcy866
selftext:
I've ad hoc built some of this (like specialist agents) as I go, but wondering if I should just submit myself to this github [https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios](https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios)

which seems to have thought it through a lot more. 

I know people in other thread were divided on how much to rely on skills. 

For someone like me with no technical or industry background in any of this, it's reassuring that other people have thought through the workflows etc and I can let that guide me.

Thanks!

comments.author: KalrexOW
comments.body: that looks like it's going to one shot your claude plan in 3 minutes XD

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: You mean it will spend tokens fast? Why would it do that? Isnt it more specialized?

comments.author: witmann_pl
comments.body:
This reminds me of the BMAD Method system for software development. At first it looked cool but the more you use it the more you realize it produces a, lot of bloated documents that you read for hours and which later clog your context window.

Personally I would rely on a set of specialist skills for the engine you use and that should be enough. For Godot I can recommend this one https://github.com/jame581/GodotPrompter

comments.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
comments.body:
What a useless repo. Kudos to the developer for releasing it, it's definitely popular, but in 5 minutes I can shit out a more useful word document for game development. Just get OpenClaw and build your own system 

I run an actual multi-agent setup for game work. About 20 persistent agents, separate sessions, own memory, working in parallel. That repo is 49 agent definition files inside one session. They're costumes, not a studio. None of them remember anything between sessions, none of them learn, and the technical-artist file after 100 jobs is byte-identical to before job 1.
The best part is the repo refutes itself. Buried mid-README they actually measured it: crank the process up and the test build wrote 30 design documents before its first line of game code, and blind reviewers plus a playtest ranked that build last of the four. The one-doc build won. Then they put "49 agents, 74 skills" on the banner anyway, because that's what gets stars. (31k of them, for a template that ships zero games. It says so proudly: the games are "deliberately not shipped here.")
What you already did is the correct order of operations. Bolting on a specialist when you hit a real problem means your process is scar tissue from your own project. Adopting theirs wholesale means inheriting process for problems you may never have, encoding their game, not yours.
If you take anything from it, take two things: run it in minimal mode if you run it at all, and keep their one genuinely good rule. A change isn't done until you've launched the game and looked at it. A passing check is not a running game.

And on the skills debate from the other thread: skills over agent files, every time. A skill is knowledge your agent can use. An agent definition is a hat it wears.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: Thanks that’s helpful. Can you share what the 20 agents are and how they work? I don’t understand how they can be “persistent”.

replies.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
replies.body:
I don't think you can have persistentcy without OpenClaw or hermes. And I think you have to fork something on Hermes for multiple agents.

For the game studio, I think I only have 6 agents, and that is way more than enough. They each get one tool, and record their lessons as they make projects.

I have an agent for blender, and individual agents for apps such as an inhouse music app, photocraft, UE(programming and game composition), UE (scene staging and animation), an a producer/ orchestrator.

replies.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
replies.body: Actually, with Claudecode you may be able to set up "seats" with a ticket system that can be tackled with its corresponding seat that has its own workspace, including tools, lessons, assets, and permissions. Each seat would have its own agents.md file, although I guess you could call it a seat file.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: Thank you, this is sort of over my head tho.

replies.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
replies.body: Paste my comments into your app and see what it says. I didnt design any of this, and I barely understand it. But it's very easy to implement if you give your agent more authority

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body: Unsure, I don't find skills files particulary useful to create unique stuff. It works for creating average, but there is no demand for average.

comments.author: wadrasil
comments.body:
I forked that project to work with bitrouter and use local llms. It made Othello and a character generator for an RPG system for godot. It is not bad for simple apps. 

It works in other harnesses and with local llms, you can also use it with a godot mcp to take screen shots. 

It might be more straightforward to have the LLM build a prototype in python and have it port the app to godot. This way it can compare against something it can use separately.
